The mission officially broke the record for the farthest any human has ever traveled from Earth, gave crew members astonishing views of the far side of the Moon — and, of course, set the stage for NASA’s first attempt to land astronauts on the lunar surface in over half a century. Now, according to a new study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters , it turns out that the April rocket launch also managed to tear a massive hole in the Earth’s upper atmosphere, as Space.com reports — a major disruption in the ionosphere that was powerful enough to throw off GPS signals. The launch “triggered shock waves and unprecedented large-scale disturbances” across North America. candidates.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
candidates.raw_excerpt: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life. To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life. "The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement. Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well. In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star , the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface. Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets . She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere. Central to the work is entropy, a concept in thermodynamics that describes the degree of disorder in a system. The universe naturally tends toward disorder; it’s why things decay. Or why your house gets messier over time — unless, crucially, you introduce extra energy into the system by tidying it up . candidates.title: Scientists Study Difference Between Men Who Pee Standing Up and Sitting Down
candidates.raw_excerpt: One key debate still swirling around men’s health: is it better to pee standing, or sitting down? It may seem like a silly question, but there is some scientific merit to the question. Previous studies have found that men with prostate issues or urinary complications could be better off sitting, pointing to the possibility that plopping down may help loosen up pelvic floor muscles. Unfortunately, the evidence available is far from conclusive — which is probably what inspired the Colombian Urology Research Group to plow ahead with a new study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics . The research, first flagged by Science Alert , took a look at the “posture adopted during voiding” of 52 male volunteers, 24 of whom stood while the rest sat. Each group went on a 24 hour “washout” break in between tests. During the examination, researchers looked at maximum urine flow rate, as well as the total volume of urine expelled in one go. Despite previous polarizing studies on the topic, this piece of research yielded a dull conclusion: it just doesn’t seem to matter. “In healthy men, voiding posture did not significantly modify the maximum urinary flow rate or voided volume,” the team wrote. The one difference between the two postures, the scientists noted, was in what might be called “acceleration.” “The sitting position was associated with a shorter time to maximum flow,” the scientists wrote, noting that it’s a “small difference that is unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Still, you never know until you try. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006 . NASA launches the Mars Global Surveyor to Mars on a Delta II rocket on Nov. 7, 1996. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions. "The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe. candidates.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission
candidates.raw_excerpt: We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life." Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024. NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet. Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens , which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. candidates.title: Hot Take: Chinese scientists create substance colder than deep space
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese scientists have created the coldest substance ever made by humans – and it's colder than deep space.

By cooling a cloud of rubidium atoms down to an equivalent temperature of 9.7 picokelvin, less than a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero, the research team achieved a milestone in quantum physics.

But first, they had to overcome a major hurdle: gravity.

On Earth, gravity constantly pulls atoms downward. Scientists can't pin the elusive little particles down. And if you can't hold them, you can't cool them.

So, the team engineered a "super fridge" – an ultracold atom physics facility – and launched it to the China Space Station. In microgravity, atoms float freely – much like the toothpaste you've seen in astronaut videos – allowing scientists to cool them to extremes impossible in terrestrial labs.

Getting the facility there was an engineering feat in itself. The original ground-based system weighed a massive 10 tonnes and came in at 20 cubic meters. The space version was shrunk down to just 500 kilograms.

Inside this compact facility, lasers trap the atoms in an optical net and slow them down using evaporative and non-adiabatic cooling techniques without needing bulky magnets.

This orbital lab up will allow scientists to develop quantum sensors and atomic clocks capable of measuring Earth's gravity in unprecedented detail, powering atom interferometers for next-generation navigation systems, and providing a fresh way to probe dark matter and the early universe.

candidates.raw_excerpt:
The world's first 4,000-meter-class airborne wind power system on Friday successfully completed a test flight in Yueyang, central China's Hunan Province, marking the first time a system of its kind has undergone a flight test in an urban setting.

During the flight, the China-made S4000 airborne wind power system conducted a series of tests to verify its stability control under complex airflow conditions and its power generation performance in complex magnetic environments.

Measuring 67 meters long, 40 meters wide and 23 meters high, the system can reach an altitude of up to 4,000 meters. It has an output voltage range of 10 to 35 kilovolts with a designed service life of 20 years.

The system uses a helium-filled platform to lift lightweight power generation modules thousands of meters into the sky, where it utilizes stable high-altitude winds to generate electricity. The electricity is then transmitted to the ground through its tether cable.

Testing in an urban environment assesses whether the system can operate safely and reliably near populated areas, Dun Tianrui, chief architectural designer of the system, told China Media Group.

As major hubs of electricity demand, cities are the ultimate target areas for the deployment of these power generation systems, said Dun.

It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572 , is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. candidates.title: Delivery Robot Causes Car Accident With Nine Injuries
candidates.raw_excerpt: At least nine bus riders were injured when a wayward delivery robot plowed into oncoming traffic in Estonia. The incident happened in the capital city Tallinn, in the middle of rush-hour traffic. As Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported , a delivery robot operated by the company Starship Technologies blundered into an intersection during a “no walk” signal, bringing it squarely into the path of an oncoming bus. Reacting to the obstacle darting out into the road, the bus driver hit the brakes, sending passengers tumbling. The driver’s quick reaction might have actually spared the robot, as the device reportedly continued on its delivery route after colliding with the front of the bus. “The robot fled, if you can put it that way,” as one Tallinn Transport official told ERR . As the spokesperson put it, the robot’s actions may legally constitute fleeing the scene of a traffic incident, meaning Starship Technologies could very well be on the hook for the incident. “If a participant in a traffic accident leaves the scene without fulfilling the obligations prescribed by law, this may constitute an offense,” the transportation official explained. It wouldn’t the company’s first brush with the law. In Arizona, a 73-year-old woman is suing the company after one of its robots allegedly pushed her to the ground, ramming into her repeatedly as she tried to get up. As for the Estonian situation, Starship’s head of operation Pepe Aaviksoo blamed bright ad boards and traffic lights, which apparently disoriented the robot’s sensors. “There are many lessons to be learned, but exceptional situations do occur,” he said. candidates.raw_excerpt: File photo of a Falcon 9 fueled for launch at pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California. Image: SpaceX. SpaceX will deploy another batch of satellites for a clandestine U.S. Space Force program on a Falcon 9 rocket to launch from California Friday afternoon. Liftoff from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base is scheduled for 4:48 p.m. PST (7:48 p.m. EST / 0048 UTC). The rocket will take a south-easterly trajectory on departure from the central California coast. The flight was originally scheduled for Nov. 1 but was delayed repeatedly, first due to delays of the Starlink 15-18 launch, and then for reasons that were not disclosed. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 30 minutes prior to launch. The mission is designated USSF-432 but is also identified as R-4 in public documents. This series of ‘R’ missions began Aug. 16 with USSF-366. More launches in the sequence followed with USSF-153 (R-2) on Sept. 10 and USSF-385 (R3) on Sept. 26. Each R launch has placed 23 satellites in orbit, according to orbital catalog entries. They are thought to be based on SpaceX’s Starshield platform, the government version of the Starlink satellite. According to Jonathan McDowell, the respected tracker of space launches, the R satellites are part of the U.S. Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting program. Officially, the Space Force has declined to provide any information about the missions. The Falcon 9 first stage booster, B1095, is making its eighth flight and is scheduled to land on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You,’ which will be stationed in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Baja California, Mexico.

candidates.title: Colorado-Based Launcher Takes Scottish Leap of Faith
candidates.raw_excerpt: LEAP a Colorado-based company, has signed a deal as it looks to develop better international launch capabilities. It plans to develop recurring launch operations at a launch site in Sutherland, located on Scotland’s northern mainland. This collaboration between LEAP and the Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE) is an interesting one given the lack of launches so far from the U.K. The MoU between LEAP and HIE was announced Nov. 5. LEAP is building a dual-use logistics network to move critical payloads anywhere on Earth “within minutes,” as well as a core service to take small satellites into orbit. Sutherland could become the network’s first launch site outside of the U.S., giving LEAP a base from which to serve European customers while supporting the development of sovereign launch capability in the U.K. Under the MoU, the two organizations intend to establish a dedicated launch development workstream focused on creating a practical pathway for LEAP launches. The MoU establishes a framework for collaboration and, while non-binding, can be interpreted as the latest sign that LEAP is strongly considering the U.K. as its European headquarters. The firm previously announced its intention to explore operations in the U.K. during Space-Comm Glasgow in 2025 and has since visited Edinburgh, Glasgow, Machrihanish, and sites around Inverness. candidates.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
candidates.raw_excerpt: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come! Ascending in the morning In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight. It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. candidates.title: Flock Cameras Got Eviscerated by the Midterms
candidates.raw_excerpt: Tuesdays midterm elections in the US were a referendum on a lot of things — the war on Iran , data centers , and the ultra-powerful tech lobby , to name just a few. In several local contests, the elections were also a crushing blow for the rising domestic surveillance industry , as voters sent automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies like Flock Safety packing. In York County, Maine, for example, a ballot measure to remove the town’s current ALPRs and require voter approval for any future installations of surveillance technology passed with flying colors, winning a 72 percent share of the vote. And in League City, Texas, a measure to “advise the city to continue police use” of ALPRs failed — albeit by a slimmer margin, with 54 percent of voters opposing the measure. As the newspaper Community Impact reported , cities like Pflugerville, Texas also passed ordinances requiring public approval before installing any facial recognition, surveillance, and AI tools that could infringe on residents’ privacy going forward. Beyond ballot measures, municipal politicians with wishy-washy messaging around Flock bans were also trounced. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. The meteorite , named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered in 2022, weighs roughly 1.8 pounds (800 grams) and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. Blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually landing on Earth, it is one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The extraordinary age and unusual mineral composition of Teghaza 001 offer a rare glimpse into the formation of Mars' early crust and how volcanic materials may have been altered by water, according to a statement from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” research leader Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California said in the statement. "One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars." A Rosetta Stone for Mars Unlike many Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 contains a distinctive combination of igneous minerals and textures that preserve evidence of its complex history. Its mineral composition resembles materials observed in Mars' southern highlands by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter . "It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." The meteorite was initially identified as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes.
